novum_candidates.description: The superstition that a black cat (Joseph) brings luck, invoked repeatedly by characters as a supposed causal force shaping the fortunes of James, Elizabeth, and Briggs.

novelty.rationale: The black-cat-luck motif is a mundane real-world superstition, not a totalizing world-altering difference from the empirical norm. The story explicitly frames it as an 'idiotic superstition' and never establishes it as an operative law of the storyworld; the outcomes (play failure, romance) unfold through ordinary human causation. There is no estranged world different from the author's empirical reality.

cognitive_validation.rationale: There is no systematic, immanent, nonsupernatural account of the cat causing luck. Insofar as luck-causation is asserted, it is presented as folk superstition and irony, not as an imaginary science or coherent social/physical mechanism. The narrative undercuts rather than validates any lawful account.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The cat and its supposed luck function as a recurring plot device that brings characters together and structures the comic reversals, so it is more than wholly incidental. However, the overriding narrative logic is a conventional romantic comedy of manners driven by human emotion and irony, not by the cat operating as a genuine novum. Its centrality is thematic/comic rather than world-governing.

novum_candidates.estrangement_rationale: The only reader-facing contrast is ironic: James contrasts superstition with being 'sane and practical' (sfev-6abf23a9b2c43e16), and the plot's outcomes ironically invert the luck belief (the play fails yet romance succeeds, per sfev-93ffa21c31ffb27a). This is comic irony, not cognitive estrangement producing a novel storyworld.
